neighbours.label: quotation marks in a summary or analysis of fiction: a character's words being quoted, as opposed to quotes from real people
fire: When Macbeth hears of his wife's death, he says, "She should have died hereafter."
In Chapter 3, Scout asks Atticus, "Do you defend them?" and he nods.
Pip feels ashamed of Joe's manners and calls his own hands "coarse" in the next scene.
Later in the play, Ophelia tells her brother, "There's rosemary, that's for remembrance."
Heathcliff, as Nelly observes, has "a sharp, cunning look" after he comes back.
Throughout the book, Holden calls nearly everyone a "phony" and avoids adults.
When the shark comes, Santiago tells himself, "A man can be destroyed but not defeated."
Jane Eyre resists Rochester's offer and declares, "I am no bird."
quiet: When the senator heard of the vote, he said, "We will appeal the decision."
In Monday's briefing, the coach told reporters, "We played hard," and he left.
The customer was angry about the delivery and called the service "slow" in the next email.
Later in the day, the mayor told her staff, "There's money for the park."
The CEO, as analysts observed, has "a strong balance sheet" after the merger.
Throughout the interview, the chef calls nearly everything "fresh" and smiles.
When the storm came, the fisherman told a local radio station, "We lost two boats."
The union rejected the company's offer and declared, "We are on strike."

notes: Top examples are plot summaries and essays on novels and plays. In probes, news and review quotes stayed under 0.03, and fiction without quotation marks reached about 0.2. Near misses have the same frame with real people quoted.
